blocks.x: Name first. Thomas Valentine.
Thomas Valentine. You have any middle name? No middle name. When did they start calling you the kid? Where did that come in?

When I came down here. Just down? When I came down here. The bass player gave me that name. T.G. Rouchon. Bass player. Oh yeah. See they was going to pick, you know when we organized the band, they was going to see what name would match, you know what I mean, for the band. You know what I mean? So T.G. Rouchon said well my name would be the best. See? So that's why they named the band after me. After me. So then after that well, see another boy he was manager of the band, Fais. Because he had the band before I came here, you see? So after this boy died, he sent for me, see for the, for coming to play with his band. So that's why they picked the name, my name.

See? We might start in just a little bit at the beginning. Give the very first facts about your life. The date that you were born. I think we have that, but just to be sure we have it all down. Uh huh. Yeah. Where were you born?
I was born in Reserva Zena.
And what was the exact date?
It was February the f-3, 4th.
February the 4th. What year?
It's uh... 19... How old are you now? We can figure...

I'm 62. 62. You'll be 63 next month. Yeah. Just about a month from today almost. Uh huh. Can you tell about your father? I know he played music and instruments. Well he, I'll tell you they had a, he used to play in a brass band. They had a brass band. Well in fact they had two brass bands out there. And the Arnold band and the Pickwick band. He used to play in the Pickwick band. They were both reserve bands, not down here. Both reserve bands.

Yeah, both reserve bands. Well first of all, what was your father's name? Peter Valdeman. Peter. He's not living is he? Yeah he's living. Well that's what I wondered. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. He's still living.
Sure. One of these times I'm coming and I'm going to let you know I'm going to take you out there.
Well yeah, someday we'll go out and we'll interview him too. Sure. Don't have to ask all about his life then you can tell him.
Yeah.
He's living. Sure he's living. How old is he about now?
Oh he's over seventy. Yeah well he'd have to be. Yeah he on pension now you know. He on pension. He's still up in reserve then. Yeah still in the same place.
Well tell us a little bit about it and then we'll ask him some more and we can think of other

questions. Well he, well you see he used to play in a band, he used to play the alto in the band. See? He used to play the alto in the band and then after that well he used to fool around with trumpet, trombone and song like that you know. He had one of them valve trombone you know what I mean? He had sliding trombone, trumpet and different things like that you know. So well and this boy, this Hall boy, daddy, well he used to play in the onward band here. See Edmund Hall daddy. Father yeah. Yeah he used to play in the onward band and well they had two different bands you see.
Yes.

So, and they used to come down here every carnival didn't play. And every carnival would come, and every time they come down here they would win the prize. Is that with your father's band? My father's band. Every time they come down here they used to wear a red, a red uniform, red outfit you know. So I used to come down here every year carnival they would come down. For eleven years when you used to have carnival they didn't have enough bands. They used to send off and get band different parts you know. Sure. You know what I mean? Different part of the country you know. Because they used to have a lot of parades. And like, not like today you see. So, well they come down here and he, well he played a long time. But after that the band, broke up you know what I mean? Band broke up. Then the fellas, fellas they organized, they had a orchestra. They had an orchestra you see. Not my daddy. He didn't have no, they didn't have no orchestra, not him. But Marshall Lawrence, he had an orchestra. He played the violets. He was, he managed the band, lead the band. And the fella used to play the trumpet. Well he got drowned.
Well was that that strip and stuff?
Yeah, yeah, well he got drowned at him you see.
What was that about?

Ooh, that band, that man. Was that after you moved down? No, that was before. That was before I moved down. That must have been a but, you know when that was? That's before the war. Before the first war. Yeah. That was before the first war. What did he play the fella that, was there only one fella that was left?
How many of them were drowned that night?
Only, only, only the trumpet player and this fella was pulling the skiff.
Yeah.

Well he was supposed to be a good swimmer, but he got drowned at him. And that, you see how terrible the bell, how the thing got, it was foggy you see. And they crossed the river. Well that's the only way, we used to cross the river to go play music on the other side you see.
Was that up at the, at the river?

Yeah, you see well they had, they had a little ferry boat you know what I mean. But it was no large ferry boat like Conair Street ferry. Yeah. But it was, it run certain time and, and, and, and, and it don't run no more. Yeah. You know certain time in the evening late you see. Yeah. Well that was, that would be for the people coming from the courthouse on the other side you see. And people from going from white you know what I mean like that too you know coming to the, to the, to the sugary farm you see. So well, that Saturday night it was kind of foggy. So they went across the river and the, the fellow that got drowned, Dejon his name was. He, he, you know how some people get frightened. Yeah. See. It wouldn't have been for that. Then none of them wouldn't have got drowned you know what I mean. But he, he turned his kiff over. You see he got frightened. Yeah. He jumped out of the kiff you see. Well quite natural when he turned his kiff over that fellow he got, his fellow was pulling the skiff. He got drowned and, and he got drowned you see. Well my, my cousin Lionel, he the drummer, the bass player. Yeah. Drummer, the bass player, the trombone player. And uh, well the kind of player lived on the other side you see. Yeah. Well he lived there you see. Well all the rest of the fellows got saved. See. Mm-hm. So, they, they saved all the instruments and everything. You know what I mean. Yeah. They saved everything you see. Cause the drum you know, long, the drum gonna float on the head you see. Long, long it don't turn over on that, why that whole head you see. In the bass you see. So what saved my cousin in the trombone player, they held onto that chain on that skiff you see. Oh yeah. And you know when the fellow getting drowned with the bill, you know if he grab you, he ain't gonna let go you know. Oh no, he ain't gonna let go. So he, that my cousin saved him, he grabbed onto my cousin you see. Mm-hm. So, well alright. So well that's settled. Well they went on like that, the band went on so. Well they was wondering why they could get another trumpet player you know. So that's why they got, uh, Mud Carey. Oh yeah.
To play trumpet.

Mud Carey came out, he used to come out, you know like on Saturdays night and play with him you see. But I tell you, now Mud Carey was a fellow, was more of a Dixieland player, you see. Yeah. Well them fellows were musical. They were strictly musical, them fellows there. All them fellows were realists, you know what I mean. Yeah. And so he'd come out on Saturdays and then he would always want the fellows to play in the style he played you see. You know what I mean. More live and jazzy like, you know what I mean. But the fellow wasn't so used to that because they strictly read music, you know what I'm talking about. So well finally they went on like that, the band went on and they played like that for a long time and so finally, you know again, the band split up. Well my cousin, well now we had a band ourselves you see, so my cousin, we organized a new band. So I got my cousin to play with me and so after I got my cousin to play with me, well the band had to split up you see. So what they did, Marshall organized a new band. He started teaching you see, youngsters you see, to teach me. Well that's a pretty good band for boys. Used to come all down here and play too you see. Used to come down, they had a great big band, all musicals you know what I mean. Well he used to come down here and go all over the country and play, Texas, different places you know. So well my cousin, he played drum with us, so he left and went to, he went to Baton Rouge, play with Toot Johnson. So well every now and then, every week, and like that, they used to send for him to come out and play. So finally after he started playing with them regular, he went up there and lived there. You see, he moved his family there and went to live there and he stayed there all the again until he died you see. So well our band, now when he left, you see we had bought, we had bought a whole lot of new instruments, a whole set of instruments. That Hall boy, Edmund Hall is the one, him and my cousin came down here and ordered the instruments at Groomhall. I had a Holton trumpet, we had a brand new Holton banjo, trombone, a whole lot of flit you know. So after this fella, after he came back, my cousin, they came back with all the instruments, brought all the instruments at night and all the boys out there you know. You know how some people be jealous you see. Man, when my cousin Edmund brought them instruments and pulled them out there, them fellas eyes stretched big like that you know. He said, how y'all gonna pay for them instruments? But we was getting paid to white. Oh we was getting paid to white, we had a good band. We were a good band, that's my mother say. We were a good band. We were a good band. So, alright. So we got the instruments. So finally we doing alright. We paid for the instruments and everything. So, alright. Edmund, he left, no the oldest brother left first, Robert left. He left the country and come down here. So after that Edmund, he left. So finally that left, Clowns playing the banjo with us you see. Well Clowns still stayed. So alright. So Clowns playing the banjo. He wasn't playing no saxophone, playing the banjo. So when you know again, he wanted to leave. So everybody leaving but me. See that left me. I was the last one. Did Herbert Hall play ever with you? No, no.
The youngest.

He never played with us because he left and went away, he went to Texas you see. He left and went to Texas. But Edmund, Robert, and Clowns, all of them we played together, we come up together you see, we played together you see. So well after that all left, well quite naturally that just left me. So now. I said well, I said it's my move now you know. So what I did Mr. Bill, I met up my mind and left. That's why I came here. I was down here living on Clio Street when this boy River, Elton, when he written on the country, a boy, his brother-in-law you see where his brother-in-law knows me. He said oh I know a fella you might get to play in your band. He told him, he said that fella called Thomas. He said oh you think he come? He said yeah you might come. So sure enough I was already down here you know. So I lived on Clio Street so the fella, I got the letter. He sent the letter out home and sent the letter back to me. So the boy explained me that I come up to go over the river you see. I had to get over on the ferry. So all I did I got the street cars like he said I went right on to the ferry you know. I got on the ferry. So he explained he said now listen, he said when you get off the ferry, if you want to ride the street car, you could ride a street car but it wouldn't be necessary because you could walk from there to Fred Street where he lived there you know. He lived in it by a message church and he told me, he said well, he said if you walk, you'll see a fire department. You know what I mean? Yeah. He said you come up to the fire department and you're tying. See, tying to your right and then when you get, when you leave the fire department right in the block they got a theater there. So he said you're tying and it comes like you're going to the woods. I did this like you say in the letter you know. So I went on and he went right straight to his house. So his wife said, told me, say, how you find, how you find out why we live that good? You, you do better if you wouldn't live here in the city. The first time I been in there all day is my life, Mr. Bill, I'm telling you. First time in my life, and I went right straight there. So, well the boy, this boy, he was working at the time, he was working for the railroad. So, well I went there at 12 o'clock, he was surprised you know, when he found me there you know. So, well, fine, well, he was talking, different things. So, I told him, I said, well I live on Kyle Street. He said, well, he asked me if I want to live with them. Well, I said, no. So, what I did, I went and live with the bass player, with Roushaw, Tiet Roushaw. I live with him. I stayed with him. I stayed on this side. So, finally, well, after that, this boy, Albert, Tom Albert's son. Oh yeah. He said, man, it would be better for you to come and live on the other side of the river, because we got all the bins on the other side, you know what I mean? See, of course, we got bins on both sides, but it would be over there, you know. You know what I'm scared of? I'm scared somebody's going to take me away from you see. Yeah. You see? Well, he's playing trambone too, you know, with Alton. So, well, I went on and I stayed. I stayed. I went over there and stayed with him. Yeah. I went over there and I stayed with him. So, finally, I moved. Up there, I moved from there and then I went and left. I got a room to myself. He said, a room. He said, a room. He said, a room. So, finally, well, then that boy, I got a wife, you see. Mm-hmm. So, all right. So, well, after that, we start, you know, the most thing we was doing when we first organized the band, we wasn't doing nothing but rehearsing, you see. We rehearsed three and four times a week, like on Sundays and everything. We could get jobs but we didn't want to take no jobs. Try and we'd get the band together, you know, everything straightened out. So, when everybody get out, nobody wouldn't have to tell nobody what to do, you see. Steve was playing trambone with us, too.
Steve, in drum?

Yeah, he first started, a little fella they called Tommy Henderson. He was a little fella playing drum with us, you see. He was a nice little drummer. So, well, we played, we rehearsed it every three times a week and then after that, we went after that, one night, it rained, it rained all day and all night. It was the Beville Park on Beville Street. Beville? Yeah, on Beville Street there. Newton, you see after you leave Tash, you see. Tash, Newton, Nunes, Ferret, Villette. And next, see, the next street, that's Beville. Was there a dance hall there?
Yeah, yeah, Beville Park used to call it. See that?

In the real park. Well, one time there used to be for colored, the colored people had it once and then after they turned it into white. And it rained all that day, you know, and we had to play a dance. And the first dance we played Mr. Billy, the first day with our band. Anybody go to the dance? Oh, the place was packed. They couldn't go home? Oh yeah, it was packed Mr. Billy, that place was packed. So, and we went there and we played that dance that night. And from that, I'm going to tell you to Mr. Billy, that one night Saturday night we played there and we'd been going and we had more work we could handle. We had more work, sometimes I'm telling you, sometimes we had so much work, I wouldn't put my shoes off for three or four nights, put them off. Just come in and look and my wife and things like that freshers would have been gone again. We used to go all about, Ponce de Toulas, we used to go everywhere and play, all over. You know what I mean? We were there in Ponce de Toulas, went to Baton Rouge, Texas, we went even to Harri, well not Harri here, or Emmet, all them places, you know what I mean? We used to play dances, you know? So, always doing good. I mean playing all on the lake, you know, every Sunday, lakes, dances down on the lake, on Sundays. And sometimes we play dances. We'll have three dances in one night. Three in one night, you see? We used to play so many hours here, so many hours there, so many hours the other, you know what I mean? That's how we used to do, you see? We had that much work, you know? Playing a lot of picnics and advertisements and so on like that. So, and we used to wear a blue blouse, you know? Blue blouse, white pants and cap. That's what we were doing, we used to wear. And everywhere we go, everybody knows. If we just see one of the fellas, they say, they say, one of you, we just saw one of you men's past year, we know it was him, you see? Because he had the same kind of uniform, you see? I got the picture, am I never sure the picture? No, I don't think so. I'm going to bring that picture to show the band.
Maybe make a copy of it sometime.

Sure, I got the whole band. You see, we took it, when we took it on Cunningham Treatment, the studio was small, you know what I mean. It wasn't big enough. But all, all, you can make, everybody on that, on the picture. I showed it to this boy, he's the manager of the band, you know? I showed it to him not long ago, I brought it to his wife. Up there he got another wife, his wife's dead now. But he got another wife. And she said, Lord, I said, Thomas, where you got that picture from? So he said, he told me, he said, Thomas, I would like to have a picture made of it. I said, yeah, you can have a picture.
Sometimes we're drilling, you can make a copy for him too.

Yeah, yeah, that's what I told him, you know what I mean? And, I mean, just like we took it, it's the same with me. I got a little small frame on the wall, and so, I'm the only one got one in picture. And, them fellas, they ain't got nothing.
Most people don't say those things.

No, they ain't got nothing. I'm the only one got them pictures. So, alright. Like, you take like the uniforms. We used to wear a uniform, we had a jacket, a blue jacket, with a dark lapel, you know what I mean? And, blue pants with stripes. And, you know what I mean? None of them fellas don't have the jacket and the pants. I'm still got them. You stayed here? And that been years ago. I even got them white pants we used to wear. Even got that. See? You know what? Sometimes boys see me, we say, man, what? See, they ain't them same pants. I said that. He said, man, I ain't long wear that. The blue shirt I would, with your head, you know? So, alright. So, well I tell you what happened. Then, the bass player, he died. The drum player, Johnny Thomas, he died. Teep Ruchon, he died. That was two fellas of the band. So, we got another boy, Alvin Clemons, we got him to play. Nice drummer, had good instruments. Good instruments, that boy, and he was a nice drummer, you know what I mean? So, well poor boy, he died too. See? So, after he died, well that made us got, I got, see, well I got away from that band. This band, the first band, the band, you know what I mean? I got away from them fellas, you see? I organized my own band then, you see? That was, that was, I got Edmund Washington, and Sammy, and uh, who was playing bass with us? Bikes? And uh, who else? Oh yeah. I even had this fella boy, Henry Harden, playing saxophone with us too. I remember we had another boy playing saxophone with us, Alito saxophone, John Smith. He died. That was three, three members we lost in our band. Have any piano? Yeah we had piano, Joe James, the same piano player. What about fan? You see, we didn't. Did fan bourgeois ever play with you? Fan? Yeah.
Where you live in? He lives out on, oh near Roman Street.

Well I'll tell you, I'll tell you, probably Mr. Billy. Fan? Yeah. He plays banjo too. Well I'll tell you, probably, probably play with him, cause you know we used to hire, we used to hire plenty of fellas like that. Sometime like a fella, you know what I mean, we'd need a fella, well we'd hire him, you know, something like that.
Did you use two trumpets? Seems like somebody told me they played trumpet with you for a while. You know who played with me? Wooden Joe. Oh yeah.

Wooden Joe played two trumpets with us? I used to, we used to play parade, we had a brass band, we had a pretty good brass band. Well, me, me, me and Wooden Joe, alright. Wooden Joe played with us a long time. And uh, Russ, he played trumpet with us at Moulin Rouge during the time of the war. He was in the Navy. Who was that then?
Russell.

Russell. Yeah. He lived over the river. He was the first guy musician, that boy then. Yeah. Oh yeah. He was playing with us too. He was playing with us the best with us, and the boy said quick you see. It's alright. He played second trumpet with me, and Love played second trumpet with me.
Oh yeah.

Yeah that's right. And I'll tell you, in all the second trumpet I had, him and Russ in love was the best two second trumpet I had. He really knows how to play second you know. Well, and uh, so uh, then that was I got uh, that boy, what that boy's name again, this fellow, he's sick now, he's in the record band, played second. Oh yeah. Rodney. Well Rodney played in the Edmund Washington place, you see, after we was working for the railroad. He, well he played with us a long time. So then after that, well, I got Edmund Washington back. When we got laid off, you see, from the job. He come back in, so well after that, well I got Mayor Paul to play with us, see. Uh huh. Got Mayor Paul, well this other boy, he played tramo, well he had stopped playing tramo altogether before he joined the church. See, now I got uh, Nelson. Yeah. Got Nelson to play with us, you know, with me, with me, and uh, so.
Who was your favorite second coronet that you ever played with? Well the. When you had two coronets, did you play the lead usually and the other fellow played? Yeah, I played the lead.

Play sort of. Yeah, yeah, I played the lead. Well I used to play, you know, I played lead some and then I let the other fellow play lead too, you know what I mean. Straight around the part. Yeah, like Love and like Russ and like this other boy, you know what I mean? She called it Over the Riverdale.
Who were the best second trumpets around town would you say in those days?

Well I'll tell you. For me, for me second trumpet player, Buddy Petey. Yeah, he's the best. Really good. Because every brass band, every brass band used to always have him to play second croquet. He used to tell me that all the time, you know. One day me and him was sitting down, you know. When I lived, I lived around for a rest of the day. And I asked him, I said, I said, what do you play? I said, what, what you playing in, in, in the brass band? I said, you play first or what? He said, no man, play second. He said, man, every time they get me, they put me on second. I said, why? I said, maybe, maybe, I said, you must be mighty good. You know what I mean? But he really was good. He really good, Mr. Bell. He really was good second trumpet player. Oh yeah. He's all right, he's good, he's good. I'm telling you. And that's hard, Mr. Bell. Yeah. And you know what's harder? Third is more harder. Third. What part is the third play? Third trumpet. Still in low harmony? Low, low, low, low. He way below the second. Oh man, that's tough, man. See, just like a, you take just like a third alto. You see like, you take like playing them fellas have a big band with four, five saxophone. They range all that music, you see. Yeah, sure. And from, you see, well, they might have five, they got five, they got second, they got third, they got fourth, they got fifth and all that. You know what I mean? But they range, they range every, every man a part. You see? Then after they get it all arranged, then they, then they rehearsal that, you see. So they can see how it's going to come out, you see. Yeah. That's hard, you see. So well, I always did prefer Buddy Petey's, you know what I mean? Because he really could play some nice sweet trumpet, you know what I mean? But so far as, then I had another fella, I had another fella, I can't call that man's name down to death. He used to live uptown there. He was the old time to play trumpet, I can't, I had him playing second trumpet with me, but he wasn't as good as the mother boys, you know what I mean? I can't call this fella none, his name none. But anyhow, so when we was playing up there, oh yeah, we'll get back to this country, Benny. I tell, when the country, we had our band, Mr. Bill, the name of our band, a fella had a drugstore. He named our band after the name of a medicine. It was Niles. Oh yeah. Yeah, name after medicine it was, you see. Now them fellas were all wealthy fellas. Well they tried to organize a band too, a whole bunch of wealthy boys, you know. I know he wasn't going to last, you see. And bought it, I mean they really bought some expenses as much, you know what I mean? Oh strictly music. They played there for a couple months and they broke the band up, you know what I mean? The wives begin to get jealous and all that old kind of stuff, you know what I mean? So, well the man named our band after. So, man named Morin, he had a bakery, you see. Well he had a pavilion to dance. Man, I can't tell you about that because that's where our first man met him. He came out there and played out there, you see. And so, Peter Lock, this fella played trouble with, with, with, with, with Erika? Peter Bocas? No, not Peter Bocas. He lived downtown there. There's a sheik. Sheik and that was. Pazjo. Pazjo. Pazjo and Mamoneta was playing again, I see, because the medium was talking on the river there one day, I see, I see, I see, ain't you playing with Mamoneta? I see, he called, he was talking with the name of the band there. I see, look at her, I see, you playing with Mamoneta, out in the, your, your band had name, you see. He said, yeah. I see, well that was our first met Mamon in the country, that's playing at the pavilion. Well we used to play there, for that man regular, you see. So, he had a clubhouse and then he had a pavilion, you see. He had the, he had the pavilion, his brother had the clubhouse, you see. So, well, so we used to play there, every Saturdays and Sundays and different things through the week. They used to go different places and play, you know. We had to join a good band, I mean really, good band. So, well, after you know boys begin to get too good so they all begin to scatter. See, everybody begin to scatter, no band no more. So, well finally they had another boy, he organized another little band out there, out in the country. Well, they had a pretty good little band, you know what I mean. So Marshall Lawrence, he organized a new band. All youngsters, you see. Well alright. The minute them boys got good, they begin to scatter. Edmund's brother, the one who went in New York, he's playing Marshall too, he's scattered. And he got one in the country, we used to play the sousaphone. Well after the band, well, another boy, he played trombone, well he stopped playing. So, well all began to, well he was the only fella that didn't left there, you see, that's trombone player. Well all the rest of the boys began to scatter, went different places, you know. And Marshall said he wasn't going to teach them no more. He said every time he get a band, put a good band, everybody jumps him, you know. So that's why they don't have no band in the country now. You see, they have bands, you know. There's still fellas up there though, that's why. Yeah, that's right, but they got rock and roll. Oh yeah. Them young kids, you know. Yeah. Rock and roll band, that's all they got. You see, got a couple of them fellas young kids. But Marshall Lawrence, last time I was there, I went there, he told me, he said, oh, Tom, he said, hey you fool with them fellas no more. He said, soon you get them fellas lined up, they all jump and leave you. You know what I mean? He said you like to, he love music, you know. He said, I'd like to play again, you know what I mean? And a different thing, you know. I'd ask him if he had his violin still, he said, yeah, I got my violin still, I got a couple of violin. So, I tell him what we going to do Mr. Bill, we going to go out there one of these days, I'll let you know. And we go and we interview him too. Yeah, I'll be fine. He's an old time, him too, you know. Oh yeah, he was. What's his full name, Marshall? Marshall Lawrence. Lawrence. Yeah, he used to be a blacksmith, mechanic, or first class mechanic. Right now he teach, he teaches school, different kind of things in school, like making different kind of furniture and so on. Oh yeah.
That's what he do now.
Manual training. Yeah, like a training school, you know what I mean? Oh, he's a really smart boy, he's a really smart fella. Really smart. So, well, he, we go out there and we'll interview him.
Yeah, I'll be fine.

Because I, one of the last times my cousin died, I went out to wake, you know, and I mean, oh, me must have talked about, one o'clock that night talking, sitting down there talking, me and my dad was talking about music, you know, he really loves music, you know. And now he'd be too glad, you know. Thank you.
All right.
It's great, man.
Thank you.
Your cousin's name is? Ninel Thomas. Ninel? Ninel.
How's that first name spelled? The M, huh? Yeah, yeah, N.
Ninel Thomas.
Yeah, Thomas. He's the one that died?
Died to Johnson.
No, not him.
When I went out there with my cousin, she was a woman.
Oh, another cousin.
Yeah, another cousin. My aunt. That's my aunt's daughter.
Is Ninel Thomas still living then?
No, he dead. He got paralyzed, two, three strokes you know.
Oh yeah.
Well he was the Tud Johnson band, he used to play Tud Johnson, you see?
Was there any other band he played with? No, he played with me and he played Marshall Lawrence.

He's playing drum when he was a little bit of a small kid, you used to have to come get him, you know what I mean? Carried drum. Was he younger than you then? Oh, he'd be older than me. He'd be older than you. Oh yeah, he's older than me.
So both of my cousins did.
Both of them used to play drums. Yeah. See? So both of them died.
See?

So he played with Tud Johnson band. And I'mma tell you the truth, Mr. Bill. That boy went away, went to Baton Rouge and you know how many times I seen him since he was there? Once. That's one, yeah. And I keep putting off to go to Baton Rouge, you know? Every time I go to this country, I tell his assistant, I say, you know what I mean? I say, I gotta go to Baton Rouge and see him, I mean. And I just keep putting off and putting off and when he knew it again, he died.
See?

I ain't even had a chance to go out there to the funeral. See? Yeah. So well, that make all of them dead. They don't have many older musicians out there now. Marshall Lawrence is the oldest they got than my daddy so far. Oh yeah, they got another fellow. Billy Wright. He's a guitar player, he used to play the guitar in the band. Well he used to play in Marshall Lawrence, he used to play a 12 string guitar.
Oh really?

Yeah, he used to play a 12 string guitar. That guy was good. Oh yeah, he's really good. And so they had another fellow used to play guitar. Let me see what his name is. He dead now. Yeah, he used to play in that band too, but he dead.
I was going to ask, Nick Allen wanted me to ask if anybody made any records up there. Do you know of any of those fellows?
No, they never made, not to my name Mr. Billy, they never made no records, not to my name.
Sometimes they used to use, well like here's one of the old cylinders, the old Edison cylinders. Some people have home machines to make them.

Uh huh, yeah, yeah. You never saw anybody take a machine around? No, I ain't never seen nobody. Cause most of all the bands that they had, that was Marshall Lawrence and their band they had, and all bands they had that. And uh, so we never did, they never did record no uh, no record to my name.
When you first moved down here, did you make any records? No, I never did. With anybody? I never had a chance. Never had a chance. Those we made across the river with the... Yeah, that time.
It's on its record.
Those were the first ones, with the Emil Barnes, the Harrison Barnes.

No, the first ones. You know, first ones. I'll tell you one thing Mr. Bill. With the band we had at the Moulin Rouge during the time of the war, boy play bass now, right now with Fat Pichon. He tell anybody. He say he made more money with us than any band he ever played with. And he said, and he, the last time I saw that boy, he told me, I was on the Boulin Rouge, he said, Kitsy, you know what I'm saying? He said, you see the band we had at the Moulin Rouge? He said, boy we all been on the top. You know, we had a real Dixieland band, you know what I mean? He said, we had a real Dixieland band, they said, what them first playing there, now ain't nothing. You see? He said, we should have been on the top. But the trouble is Mr. Bill, when you don't meet the right kind of people.
Yeah, sometimes. You don't get the breaks.

Yeah, you don't get that break. You know what I'm talking? But every time that boy see me he talk that same thing, you know what I mean? And so, and you know, playing together so long, you see, together, you see? And 15 years we played there, you see, in that one place. You see? Well, that's by playing so long in one place nobody don't know nothing about you, you see? In fact, well, we used to play a lot over here when they had a lot of dance halls. See, when I was living down here on Annette Street with this Ruchon, you know what I mean? Keith Ruchon, well, he knowed everybody over here. Well, we used to play all them banquets. We used to play all the dances, different things like that, you know? Played carval parade, play on the trucks and so on like that, you know? We used to get jobs on both sides of the river, you know? A lot of work, you know, we used to get. So, but the trouble, we never just had the chance to meet the right kind of people. You see, I'll tell you the trouble, Mr. Bill. The people in this city here, since I've been here, I'll tell you the truth. I'll tell you like them friends talking about writing a book. I could write a book myself. You see? You know what I mean? Because the people here, Mr. Bill, they're not like a lot of people. They hide things from you. They keep it away from you. You know what I mean, Mr. Bill? Yeah. They don't want you to have it. You know what they do? They do like the ox. You know, you give the ox hair, and all he don't eat, before he let the other ox eat it, he lay on it. Really? I never knew. Well, that's right. That's how these fellas will do. Now, look. Them fellas know we had a good band. They know it, you see? But they would never give us the credit. They know we had a good band. See? Because I tell you what we used to do. We used to, when we were advertising on the truck, them days when we used to advertise on the truck, every Sunday we used to advertise on the truck. We used to play at the Saint-Soup. I played with Connish too. Connish played Tramon with me too. Man, Connish, he did not. We used to play different places all over the city. We used to play. We used to play all the lawn parties, all downtown, you know what I mean? Different things like that. But the fellas, just naturally, if anything would come up, and if anybody would ask, but our band, they make the people be that don't know nothing about it.
Yeah.

That's how that is. You see? They just wouldn't let us, you know what I mean, into nothing. You know what I'm talking about? But I'll tell you one thing, Mr. Bill. One thing about it. I'm glad I'm not like a lot of people. With all that after all, Mr. Bill, people used to come to me. White people would come to me, ring me up and come at my house and say, say, kid, I'd
like to hire for Saturday night.

I said, well, I'm going to tell you the truth. I said, I'm really sorry. I said, I couldn't accept the job. I said, because I'm working. He said, well, you think you could get us a band? I told him, yeah. You know what I mean? And after I tell him that, he said, kid, I'm going to leave it up to you. And I never disappoint him. Anybody wanted a band and I couldn't work, I'd get them a band. I'd ring up, you know, got the phone, I'd ring them up. I'd say, well, listen, I got a job such and such a place. And if you want to talk to the people, I said, you're welcome. I said, and if you want the job, I said, you'll make your own price. You know what they're telling me? Okay, it's all right. You make the price. You know what I mean? I'll even make the price for them and fellas go right on the job. It never blows me up. That's one thing about it. But the fellas, all the bands I ever hire and all the white people, they saw them bands was my bands. Oh, yeah. You know? Because a fella not long ago asked me, say, kid, say, oh, I'm going to all them bands you had, what'd become of? I said, man, I said, not all my bands. I said, all them bands dead now. You know what I mean? Sure. He said, well, you sure used to get a lot of bands with different people. You know what I mean? And a lot of people offered to pay me and all that kind of stuff. I wouldn't even accept their money, you know what I mean? And I'd give them a first job. Them fellas never would offer me a nickel or, say, treatment or nothing. I wouldn't even ask him for nothing. No. I wouldn't even ask him for nothing. No. They had a boy over there, old man Humphrey, George Humphrey's son. A nice white boy. We used to play for that theater over there, Folly Theater. We used to play three times a week, advertising the truck. You see, we'd go around town, you see, and then come back and make the ferry, you see. Every ferry, we'd come back and wiggle around and meet the people, come off the ferry. So this white boy heard our band. And he came to the truck. He said, I've been listening to this band. They all advertised three times a week. I said, yeah. He said, I've been listening to this band. I've been wanting to get, you know what I mean, get in touch with you. He said, because I could get a lot of work for you. And sure enough, Mr. Bill, that white boy, I gave him a card. He said, you going to yell for me, Mr. Bill? That boy got more jobs for you. Woo! Man, we got so much we couldn't play him. All them fraternities, uptown. All them fraternity clubs. On this side? On this side of the river. I mean all up on St. George, everywhere. I mean beautiful. Even in the goal room. I played in the goal room too. I played in the, yeah, I played. Miley All Hotel, Jones Hotel. You know the only hotel I haven't played in? That hotel right down on Cunhaire Street there. That's a new one, that one. Yeah, the New Orleans. Well, and then it got one uptown there. I had a chance to play in there, but I couldn't play because we had a job. But I've been playing in most of all them hotels they got in the city, you see, hotels, you see, for different, and this boy used to get it. And now he'd get the job, but you'd never see him though. He'd just ring him and say, say kid I got jobs in such a street such a place. And you'd never see him. He wouldn't, but you're talking about a nice boy. So after that, well he was, well he began to study law, you know, you're going to be a lawyer. So he told me he used to travel all over, you know, he used to tell me all the time, I said, kid, he said, you know they got places I have went, he said, if I just could get your band in. He said, y'all make a bail of money. Now what he told me? He said, y'all make a bail of money. People don't have the music, the kind of music, you know what I mean, we play, you know what I'm talking about? Them days, you know, Mr. Bill. He said, man, you'll make a bail of money. He said, well I'm sure sorry. So he told me, he said, well kid, he said, I'll have to let go now, I said, because I'm studying law now and I'm going to be busy. I told him, I said, well I'm going to tell you, I really enjoy it. I really appreciate it too. So he got up. I done been to his office, he got an office down on Common Street there. I went there, oh, this year it was. I went, that man, I mean look, that boy was so glad to see me. He just grabbed me and hugged me and then, oh, he said, man, where the devil you been at? You know what I mean? He's telling all the girls working in the place. He said, you see that fella there? He said, that's a fine fella. He said, I used to be the manager, all them girls said, sure now? He said, sure. They said, they had a fine band. And he said, how you making nothing out here? I said, I'm doing pretty good. He said, I'm sure he's sorry to let you all down. You know what I mean? I said, I don't know. I said, quite that. I said, you got your business now, you got my business. I said, you couldn't fool with it. You know what I mean? But it was a nice, it was a nice white boy.
Well, did you ever have any other day jobs in those days? Or did music keep you busy?

Mr. Bill, I didn't have to do nothing but play music. I didn't do nothing but play. That's how I used to live off it then. You see, because everything was cheap. Well, we used to make our territory with the bill. We wouldn't make, in them days, we wouldn't make no less than $55, $60, $70 a week. No less. Playing several nights a week.
That's right.

I'm telling you. And now you take, you take raw depression times. When depression first strike, yeah, well, things was kind of a little stiff. But after, after the president, you know what I mean, got this WPA business, you know what I mean? Looked like the people was giving more entertainment than before. You know what I mean?
Did you ever belong in that WPA band?

No, I never did. No, I never went to that band at all. Never did. I didn't even try to get in it, you know what I mean? Yeah. So, and them cats had a racket in the house, you know what I mean? You know what I mean? Their friendship finished, you know what I mean?
I think so, yeah.

Oh, I know. I know. So, and so, well, we played, we had more work than we could play. We had enough work to give three and four bands. We'd give them, give them job. I had to give Howard job. Oh, so many fellas, you know. And the same, you see the same fella played trumpet with the E. Rekker band there. Pazio.
Yeah.

Every time me and him would talk, he said, what's the matter, kid, you don't get no more parade? He said, man, I like to play your job. You pay good. I like to get more money than what they get. And, and, and, and, well, they just begin to get a little bit more money now. But I used to get more money than they get. I'd be just getting three dollars, two dollars, something like that. I don't know what they was getting. I used to get more than that for them all the time, you know what I mean? And sometimes I ring them out to them, I tell them, I said, I said, Ray, I got a parade, I got a funeral for you. I got a parade for you. I said, how much are you? Oh, someone, someone. I said, man, I tell him straight. I said, man, I can get more. Oh, he told me straight. Oh, man, don't overdo this thing. I said, man, I'm telling you the truth. He said, you know, a lot of them fellas, you take a lot of people in Moreira, the boys in Moreira, you know, like all the boys raised up together, like somebody die or something. Well, they would go around and pick up money, Mr. Bill, regardless how many organizations it be belongs to, but they just pick up the money, give them, give the fella a ban, you know what I mean? Well, they pick them money up, well, I know they going to pick that money up, it's just as cheap, I charge them. Because I know they ain't going to take that money out, but left they going to drink it up. You know what I mean? So I try to get as much as I can, you know what I mean? So, well. Did you ever have any manager or just did your own booking? I had no manager, never had no manager, but that white boy.
Because that one fella helped, but he wasn't really your real manager.

No, no, just get the job, you know, by him going to school, you see. You know, used to go to different schools, you see. So, but I never had no manager, no real manager, you know, like some band. But if I had a manager, you know what I mean, we would. Did you ever keep a little book?

I know Harrison Barnes has a little book that he kept all the dates in to tell just when they were playing how much money they got for each date and everything. No, I don't have. When he played with Chris Kelly. No, I don't have that. You never did keep it?

I don't have. I might have some old, I bet I got some old contract home. Some old one, you know, way back. I bet I got still got some. You see some of those real old contracts. Yeah, I got some old one there in a box. And so I tell you, well, we didn't never had no, no, no, no body to, you know what I mean, but we managed our own self, you see. Well, in fact, we didn't need nobody because we getting more, you know what I mean? We getting more jobs. We could do our own self, you know what I mean? And so that lady over there, well, we didn't had, them dates didn't had phones like we got now. So we're lucky this boy we was playing with, well, he was living right by the Methodist Church and the lady had a store, grocery store, well, had a phone there. Well, she's very nice. Anybody want us, she call us. And tell us something that you want to watch all at the phone and you know what I mean? And so we were here to disturb you know what I mean? But she said it was all right, you know what I mean? So we got out.
I was going to ask, speaking of that Methodist Church, did the Catholic Church ever have any of the bands for the Catholic funerals in the old days?
No, no, no, no, no, no band for, I don't remember, I don't remember that.
Just Methodist and Baptist? Yeah, just Baptist.
I never, Catholic don't never hardly have bands for nobody.
They don't now, I wondered in the old days.
No, I don't remember, maybe before I came here, you know what I mean? Maybe before I came here, but since I've been here I don't remember then.

I wondered what kind of music they had in the churches too when you were a boy up in Reserve, did you belong to one of the churches up there? Catholic. You belonged to the Catholic Church? Yeah, the Catholic, well they had piano, they had a piano.

Yeah, they had that, they had that in the church. They had a piano. They had no organ them days, you know, they had a piano. So, but the Catholic people never did have no bands like the Baptist people, different organizations. Don't care what kind of organization you belong to, but they never had no band. See, but most of the other people, the Baptist people in different clubs, you see. Well, them days they had a lot of clubs, you know, different kind of clubs, you know, women's club, men's club, and all those young men.
They still have some.

And all that, they got a few now, but them days they had more than that. They used to have parades, men, parade on both sides, and they had plenty of bands. For sure. And funerals, oh, Mr. Bill, I'mma tell you the truth. Is there a funeral, two and three funeral, every, every week. Every week. I got scared. I said, who? I said, I'm going back where I come from. People die here too much than me. I swear to God, Mr. Bill, yeah, that's right. Yeah, it wouldn't scare you at first. I'm telling you. Yeah. And man, it looked like, oh man, sometimes people die so much. Oh. So, I told the boy, I'm going to go back where I come from. I said, the boy, I said, well, it makes no difference if you're going to die, you're
going to die there, die all the same, you know what I mean? I said, yeah, but they die so fast.
And the people are dying, ooh, they really die.
And every time somebody die, they have a band.
Sometimes they have two, three, two, three bands, you see?
Yeah. Because they're my funeral.

Murray Henderson, when Murray Henderson died, you know how many bands they had? They had all the bands in the city. That must have been about 12 or 14 bands. Had all the bands. They had the biggest funeral they ever had. Who was it again? Murray Henderson. Murray Henderson. Yeah, got the Undertaker over there on Tash.
Oh, over there.

Yeah, that's right. The old man died. I mean, they had every band in the city. Every band there in the city. They must have about 10 or 12 bands. That's right. And that was the biggest funeral they had in history. You see? Here. You know what I mean? I don't know if it was elsewhere, but I know here, you see? Yeah, I better cry. And so, ooh, Mr. Bill. You talking about people. Man, there's some people behind that, behind that funeral there. And the second line, they know that, oh, Lord, man. Ain't nothing like it is there today. Yeah. See? So, the people today, the youngsters, the younger people today, they don't appreciate music no more. You know what I mean? People them days, music, sure, man, if you just blow any kind of horn, man, just hit on tin can, people be running out to look and see, you know what I mean? They don't wear them no more now, you know what I mean? They even don't take effect on people no more, music, you know what I mean? In fact, they youngsters now, they like old rock and roll music, you know? They like that, you know what I mean? But so far, good music, they don't appreciate nothing like that.
No.

And the people used to follow the band from the startin' to the finish. That's right. From the startin' to the finish. You go all the way to the graveyard, okay, you go up to Gretna, they go, go to Gretna, and back, you see? And all, and Eddie Jackson, you see, when Eddie Jackson was playing in the brass band, you could hear him for miles, you see? That's right, yeah. And them youngsters really know why they had to say, oh, they, they, somebody had blocks from here. They know, because they used to hear him. They hear him, you know what I mean? They hear that instrument and why they don't hear the others, you know what I mean?
He came from over the river too, didn't he?

Yeah, he came from over the river. He used to live on, I tell you where he used to live, he used to live on, over the track there, he's right there on, Frank Boyle's got a garage, right across the street there. That's Hancock's. Yeah. That's Hancock's.
Well I was going to ask about some of the other musicians over there. Did you ever play with Peter Boccage much? Any of the Boccage brothers?

No, I never did play with, Boccage, yeah, I had a boy who used to play with me, play saxophone. Oh that's right, I heard him once with you. Yeah, Wilford Boccage, he played with me. His brother Leonard Boccage, he played banjo with me too once. He didn't play that long with me. Well he used to play with Son Allen. Yeah. See, he used to play with Son Allen then, you see.
Did you ever play in the Allen brass band?

Yeah, I played, I played in Allen's band. Then after that I played, I could have played twice in that band. Two Conval Street I played, one of the old band there. He was playing parades over here on Conval. So that Conval he wanted me to play, and I mean this boy, Tom Albert boy, he said, Albert. So he wanted us to play a parade with him. Remus Matthews, you know, was playing drums. So I told him, I said, this boy told me that the job was playing $25, you know what I mean? I said, I said, Lucia, we call him Lucia. I said, Lucia, I said, listen, I said, man, I said, that job pay more than that. I said, man, Paul told me they getting $33 or $32, you know what I mean? I said, how they getting $32? I said, no, he getting, I said, getting more than that. So soon up, all them boys telling me, they said, man, man, I wish I could play some kind of instrument. Man, I'll go make that money. I said, no, I said, y'all just don't know. I said, that's some blood money there. I said, people get through walking, you know what I mean? I said, all right, I wouldn't play the job. So finally, well, Remus Masters, he played, and this boy, Lucia, he played the tramboy, you see, went to play with old man Allen. All right. So when they played the combo parade, and they come to find out the job was paying more than $25. It's all right. So Lucia said, he told me when he came back next, when he went back to work, he told me, he said, say kid, you know one of them? He said, you sure they told me he was paying more than that? I said, I too. I said, man, long you been playing the parade, you don't know no better, man. He said, so old man Allen, his eyes was bad, you see. Now he's paying off, you see, paying off the fella, and he give him $20 over the money. And now, sure you know, he said, our kid said, sure, he beat me out of my money, and I was honest, I give him his $20 back. You know what I mean? He said, I'll give him his $20. He said, I could have kept it. He said, man, you're the man that paid $25, and the job paid $31 or $32, something like that. You know what I mean? Plus, now all right, that was plus, one or two men was missing in the band. They're supposed to have 12 men, you know what I mean? They didn't have the full band. I'll be there 10. You know what I mean? So all right, with all that money, old man Allen kept that.
You see?

So now they come and tell me. So Remus, Remus, he wouldn't take his money. He wouldn't take the money. He went to the union. So the union made him pay, paid him his full, you know what I mean, schedule, you know what you call it, full money. See, the $30, or $32, $30 was what it was and all. So Remus got disgusted. Last job I played, I played with John Casme. I didn't play the gang of that, because I used to give John a lot of parades too, you see, and things fumes too. So the last one I played was uptown, way uptown for the dried club I believe, dried convo club or something. But way uptown they played for that, I'll be playing for that same club still, eh?
Maybe a parade start up at Audubon Park. Yeah, we up there somewhere.
Well that's the same club, but all right. So Remus told me, told me, say, kids, you know, me and him going home that evening, he
said, you know what I'm saying, I believe I'm going to stop fooling with these people.

He said, before I get myself in trouble. He said the fellas get fellas to play with them. If the fella come in the band, he hogging, he telling another fella what he ain't doing and he's not doing nothing, you know what I mean? He said, I believe I'm going to change my way of living. I said, what you mean? He said, man, I'm going to join church. And sure enough, he went and joined church. He gave up his? Yeah, his wife was special, you see. Well he joined, so he joined, not, not special. So he went and joined church. And he stopped playing all together.
Did he play in the church? Somebody told me he played in the church. Yeah, he played in the church.

Yeah, I meet him, look, every time I meet him, he's working on the ferry boat, you see. And every time I cross on the ferry boat, he says, sir, sir kid, when you coming up? I said, well, first chance I get, I said, I'm coming up. So once, two Sundays I went. I played in the church, I played the trumpet, he played the drum. Later played the piano. And a fellow played the guitar, electric guitar. He played nice, nice, nice guitar too. And I mean, he had really nice church, but I enjoyed it, you know? So, I played there with him. So next time I went again, and I played again. So I didn't go no more. But every time he'd see me, he'd ask me when I'm coming back. And when the pastor would see me, he always invited me. Sam's the town, I said, when you're coming back? We really enjoyed that. He said, you can come and play any time you get ready. You know how it is, you're playing the church. You don't play no dance song. You're playing nothing but him. I said, well, quite nice. I said, I really knows that, you know what I mean? You're not supposed to play. You know what I mean? I said, well, poor boy, he died, you know, before I had a chance to go back, you see? I told him I was going to come back, you see? So I never had a chance to go back and he died. And so, but John, but after he quit, I quit, you see? I quit John, you know what I mean? John wanted me to play with him all together, you see? But the only thing I didn't like with John's band, his band wasn't organized enough for me. You see, he pick up one fella here, one fella there, and the fellas come in, some of the fellas come in there, Mr. Billy Ogden, you know what I mean?
I remember you told me once about how they-

Yeah, man, that old boy Manny, or what it was, Manny Gabriel, he come in there, he ogden, he. Poor Joe Nicholas without disturbing him, poor Joe Nicholas. He want to come talk with Joe Nicholas and Joe, with Joe Nicholas. That man could, who? That man should play parade by himself. That's why they call him Wooden Joe. So, he's got about three or four trumpets. He break the line and go up there and tell the fella what then told Joe Nicholas, what he ain't doing. And buoy me up, you know what I mean? So, I told him, I said, listen, I wouldn't tell him nothing that day. So, we had to play a funeral parade in something over the river for the young men over the river there, you know? So, when I came there, all the boys was sitting on the porch, you know? On the gallery there by the hall, you see? So, first man I seen Manny Gabriel, I got mad. Soon, angry, you know, soon I seen him, you know? Because I know it's going to be some more, but you know what I mean? So, finally, well, soon I got up there, I started to go back, you know? Remus said, no, don't do that. You know what I mean? So, he said, I said, you here back, you back here again? I said, let me tell you something. I said, of course, I said, listen, this band is not my band. I said, John is the manager of this band. I said, but I'm going to tell you. I said, you know what I told him to be? I said, look, don't get the wrong idea that I'm trying to take advantage of you because you're on my side of the river. He said, I'll tell you that on your side, you know? I said, look, you're going to play the saxophone today or else if you don't play at all. I said, and you're going to stop going, stopping the fellas from playing. I said, and the fellas working and you not working. I said, you know what's going to happen? I said, suppose everybody just take down. I said, what the music going to be at then? I said, that'd be rotten. You know what I mean? It's all right. He played that day. He ain't all good. So, John fired him. John got rid of him.
